newsitem.title: UK: BBC and ICL join forces for BBC Online service.
newsitem.headline: BBC and ICL join forces for BBC Online service.

text.p: The British Broadcasting Corporation on Thursday unveiled an alliance with information technology company ICL to develop a commercial BBC online service that will be available over the Internet.
The venture, which has the working title BBC Online, will provide a BBC-branded web service and is targeted for launch on the global computer network in early 1997.
It will be built around popular BBC radio and television programmes and magazines and will cover news, sport, information and entertainment.
The project between BBC Worldwide, the corporation's commercial arm, and ICL, controlled by Japan's giant Fujitsu Ltd, will initially run until the end of 1999.

"This pioneering relationship with ICL is an important step in the transformation of the BBC from a bi-media to a multimedia organisation," BBC Worldwide chief executive Bob Phillis said in a statement.
"BBC Online's priority is to provide an Internet service that is easy to us and easy to enjoy," he added.

The project aims to provide fast and simple Internet access through a high-performance BBC-branded software package and access service. The move is designed to position the BBC as one of the UK's leading online service providers.
The BBC will supply the creative content while ICL will be responsible for providing the systems integration services, as well as technical expertise.

BBC Online is subject to regulations that ensure no public funds are used to finance any of BBC Worldwide's commercial ventures. Revenue generated by BBC Worldwide is reinvested into the BBC's licence fee funded programmes and services.
The licence fee is a tax which must be paid by anyone with a television receiver.

BBC Director-General John Birt last month called for an above inflation hike in the annual television licence fee, which currently stands at 89.50 pounds ($140) for a colour service. The licence fee provides the BBC with some 1.8 billion pounds in annual revenue.

Birt's call for a higher licence fee met with a frosty response from politicians and the BBC is under pressure to increase revenue from its commercial activities. Net benefit from commercial ventures was 77 million pounds in 1995/96.

As part of its commercial expansion the BBC is in joint venture talks with rival pay television groups BSkyB and Flextech about the launch of new subscription channels based on BBC programming. ($1=.6412 Pound)
